passages.t: ‘You have rejected us, O God’, and ‘With God we will perform with valor’
passages.happening:
The heading is one of the longest in the Psalms. It speaks of David's wars with the Arameans, “and Joab returned and struck down 12,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt” (verse 1).

Yet the psalm begins with defeat. “You have rejected us, O God; You have broken us; You have been angry; restore us!” (verse 1). The land is like ground split open by an earthquake: “Heal its fractures, for it is quaking” (verse 2).

Then God answers. “God has spoken from His sanctuary: ‘I will triumph! I will parcel out Shechem and apportion the Valley of Succoth’” (verse 6). He names the tribes of Israel as his own, and the enemy nations as his servants (verses 7 and 8).

The people still ask who will lead them (verse 9). The psalm ends in trust. “Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless. With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies” (verses 11 and 12).
passages.hearers:
The battles are told in 2 Samuel 8 and 1 Chronicles 18. The numbers differ. The heading says Joab killed 12,000 Edomites. 2 Samuel 8 says David struck down “eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt” (2 Samuel 8:13), and 1 Chronicles 18:12 says the same of Abishai. Readers explain this in different ways: different stages of one campaign, different commanders credited for the same victory, or a copying slip in a number. None is certain, and these notes leave it open.

There is another puzzle. The heading speaks of victory, but the psalm begins in defeat. Some think it was prayed during the campaign, when Edom struck while the army was far away, before the victory came. Others think the heading tells how later readers linked the psalm to David.

In God's speech, Shechem and Succoth were places tied to Jacob's return to the land. Judah is called God's ‘scepter’, recalling Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:10). ‘Moab is My washbasin’ makes a proud nation into a humble bowl for washing feet. Throwing a sandal over Edom may mean claiming it as one's own, since a sandal was used in land deals (Ruth 4:7).
passages.later:
Verses 5 to 12 appear again, almost word for word, in Psalm 108, joined to the end of Psalm 57.

Paul learned the lesson of verse 11 the hard way: “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
passages.asks:
‘The help of man is worthless’ does not mean people are useless. It means they cannot save you in the end. Only God can.

This psalm was given ‘for instruction’, the heading says. It teaches a people what to do after a defeat: tell God the truth, listen for his promise, and go on with him. Where have you been ‘broken’, and what would it mean to say verse 12 there?
